citation.title: Average treatment effects in the presence of unknown interference

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 3.1, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] Consider a sample of $n$ units indexed by the set $\mathbf{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An experimenter intervenes on the world in ways that potentially affect the units. The intervention is described by a $n$-dimensional binary vector $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n) \in \{0, 1\}^n$. For short, we refer to $z_i$ as unit $i$'s treatment. Each unit has a function $y_i : \{0, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ denoting the observed outcome for the unit under a specific and potentially counterfactual intervention. In particular, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ is the response of $i$ when the intervention is $\mathbf{z}$. We refer to the elements of the image of this function as potential outcomes. Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (z_1, \ldots, z_{i-1}, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_n)$ denote the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. The potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ can then be written as $y_i(z_i; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. Throughout the paper, we assume that the potential outcomes are well-defined. The experimenter sets $\mathbf{z}$ according to a random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$. The probability distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the design of the experiment. The design is the sole source of randomness we will consider. Let $Y_i$ denote the observed outcome of unit $i$: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. As above, $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ denotes $\mathbf{Z}$ without its $i$th element, so $Y_i = y_i(Z_i; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$. [No interference: Section 3.2, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] It is conventional to assume that the potential outcomes are restricted so a unit's outcome is only affected by its own treatment. That is, for any two assignments $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, if the treatment of a given unit is the same for both assignments, then the outcome for that unit is also the same. This no-interference assumption admits a definition of the treatment effect $\tau_i$ for unit $i$: $\tau_i = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is any element of $\{0, 1\}^{n-1}$. [Definitions 1 to 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 1. Under no interference, the average treatment effect (ATE) is the average unit-level treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i$. The assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect is $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i}) = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 2. An assignment-conditional average treatment effect is the average of the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effects under a given assignment: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. [Definition 4: p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] DEFINITION 4. The average distributional shift effect (ADSE) is the average difference between the conditional expected outcomes for the two treatment conditions: $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Interference indicator: Section 4, p. 680 (PDF p. 8)] We say that unit $i$ interferes with unit $j$ if changing $i$'s treatment changes $j$'s outcome under at least one treatment assignment. We also say that a unit interferes with itself even if its own treatment does not affect its outcome. The indicator $I_{ij}$ denotes such interference: $I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_j(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_j(\mathbf{z}') \text{ for some } \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \{0, 1\}^n \text{ such that } \mathbf{z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}'_{-i}, \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Definition 5 (Interference dependence): p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ where $d_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I_{\ell i} I_{\ell j} = 1 \text{ for some } \ell \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ The sum $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ gives the number of interference dependencies for unit $i$. [Interference counts: p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ij}$ and $C_p = \left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^p\right]^{1/p}$. We write $C_\infty$ for the limit of $C_p$ as $p \to \infty$, which is the maximum $c_i$ over $\mathbf{U}$. [Asymptotic regime: Section 5, pp. 681–682 (PDF pp. 9–10)] We consider an arbitrary sequence of samples indexed by their sample size. The samples are not assumed to be drawn from some larger population or otherwise randomly generated. All quantities describing the samples, such as the potential outcomes and experimental designs, have their own sequences also indexed by $n$. But we leave the indexing implicit as no confusion arises. [Definition 6: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) and Hájek (HÁ) estimators are $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i}{p_i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - Z_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, where $p_i = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ is the marginal treatment probability for unit $i$. [Assumption 1: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] We assume throughout the remainder of the paper that the experimental design and potential outcomes are sufficiently well behaved, as formalized in the following assumption. ASSUMPTION 1 (Regularity conditions). There exist constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ in the sequence of samples: A (Probabilistic assignment). $k^{-1} \le \Pr(Z_i = 1) \le 1 - k^{-1}$, B (Outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^q] \le k^q$, C (Potential outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})|^s] \le k^s$ for $z \in \{0, 1\}$. [Assumption 2: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Restricted interference). $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = o(n)$. [Bernoulli design: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] We call this a Bernoulli randomization design, and it satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{z_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - z_i}$ for some set of assignment probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ bounded away from zero and one. [Complete randomization: p. 684 (PDF p. 12)] $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} \binom{n}{m}^{-1} & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$ where $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. We call the design complete randomization. [Paired randomization: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] It is implicit that the sample size is even so that all units are paired. Let $\rho : \mathbf{U} \to \mathbf{U}$ describe a pairing so that $\rho(i) = j$ indicates that units $i$ and $j$ are paired. The pairing is symmetric, so the self-composition of $\rho$ is the identity function. The paired randomization design then satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 2^{-n/2} & \text{if } z_i \ne z_{\rho(i)} \text{ for all } i \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Notation the paper uses without defining] The paper does not define $\mathcal{O}_p$, $o_p$, 'consistent' or 'root-$n$ consistent'. The proof of Lemma A5 (Supplement A, p. 4) uses $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$ in the sense that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $\kappa$ and an $N$ such that $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. 'Consistent for' an estimand means that the difference between the estimator and the estimand (both sequences in $n$) converges in probability to zero; 'root-$n$ consistent' means that this difference is $\mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5})$. Supplement A is the separate file 'Supplement A: Proofs' (41 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPA) and Supplement B is 'Supplement B: Simulation study' (21 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPB); their page numbers are their own printed page numbers, which equal their PDF page numbers. In the main article the printed page number is the PDF page number plus 672.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Lemma A12: the hypergeometric laws of $T_i$, the likelihood-ratio identity and the resulting bound, corrected; Lemma A12 as stated
canonical_claim.location: Supplement A, pp. 9–10: Lemma A12 and its proof
canonical_claim.statement: [Corrected step] Under complete randomization with $m$ treated units out of $n$ ($1 \le m \le n - 1$), fix $i$ with $\reflectbox{c}_i \le \min(m, n - m)$ and let $r_i = \reflectbox{c}_i - 1$ (the number of units other than $i$ that interfere with $i$), so that $T_i = \sum_{j \ne i} I_{ji}Z_j$ is the number of treated units among $r_i$ fixed units. Then, for $t \in \{0, \ldots, r_i\}$ and $z \in \{0, 1\}$: $\Pr(T_i = t) = \binom{m}{t}\binom{n - m}{r_i - t}\binom{n}{r_i}^{-1}$ and $\Pr(T_i = t \mid Z_i = z) = \binom{m - z}{t}\binom{n - 1 - m + z}{r_i - t}\binom{n - 1}{r_i}^{-1}$. If $r_i = 0$, then $T_i = 0$ surely and $\frac{\Pr(T_i = 0 \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(T_i = 0)} = 1$. If $r_i > 0$: $\frac{\Pr(T_i = t \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(T_i = t)} - 1 = \frac{r_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)(n - r_i)}\left[\Pr(Z_i = z) - z\frac{t}{r_i} - (1 - z)\frac{r_i - t}{r_i}\right]$, the expression within brackets is strictly between $-1$ and 1, and $\left|\frac{\Pr(T_i = t \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(T_i = t)} - 1\right| \le \frac{r_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)(n - r_i)} \le \frac{\reflectbox{c}_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)(n - \reflectbox{c}_i)} \le \frac{\reflectbox{c}_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)\min(m, n - m)}$. [Lemma A12, unchanged] Under complete randomization, for any $i \in \mathbf{U}$ such that $\reflectbox{c}_i \le \min(m, n - m)$ and any $z \in \{0, 1\}$: $\max_{\mathbf{z} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i}}\left|\frac{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z} \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z})} - 1\right| \le \frac{\reflectbox{c}_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)\min(m, n - m)}$, where $\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i} = \{\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^{n-1} : \Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}) > 0\}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Assignment vectors affecting a unit: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i = (I_{1i}Z_1, I_{2i}Z_2, \ldots, I_{ni}Z_n)$. The vector is defined so that its $j$th element is $Z_j$ if unit $j$ is interfering with $i$, and zero otherwise. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i$. The definitions have the following convenient properties: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z}) = y_i(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i)$ and $y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = y_i(z; \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})$. [Alpha-mixing coefficient: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For two random variables $X$ and $Y$ defined on the same probability space, let $\alpha(X, Y) = \sup_{x \in \sigma(X),\, y \in \sigma(Y)} \left|\Pr(x \cap y) - \Pr(x)\Pr(y)\right|$, where $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ denote the sub-sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. The coefficient $\alpha(X, Y)$ is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The maximum is $\alpha(X, Y) = 1/4$. [Definition 9 (External and internal average mixing coefficients): p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For the maximum values of $q$ and $s$ such that Assumptions 1B and 1C hold, let $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\left[\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)\right]^{\frac{q-2}{q}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\alpha(Z_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})\right]^{\frac{s-1}{s}}$, where $0^0$ is defined as zero to accommodate the cases $q = 2$ and $s = 1$. [Assumptions 5 and 6: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] ASSUMPTION 5 (Design mixing). $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = o(n)$. ASSUMPTION 6 (Design separation). $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = o(n)$. [Definitions A2 and A3: Supplement A, p. 9] DEFINITION A2. Let $m = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Z_i$ be the element sum of $\mathbf{Z}$ (i.e., the number of treated units). REMARK. Complete randomization implies that $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ with probability one for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. DEFINITION A3. Let $\reflectbox{c}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ji}$ be the number of units interfering with unit $i$. (The paper prints this symbol as a reflected italic $c$; it is written $\reflectbox{c}_i$ here.) [Lemma A12: Supplement A, p. 9] Under complete randomization, for any $i \in \mathbf{U}$ such that $\reflectbox{c}_i \le \min(m, n - m)$ and any $z \in \{0, 1\}$: $\max_{\mathbf{z} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i}}\left|\frac{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z} \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z})} - 1\right| \le \frac{\reflectbox{c}_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)\min(m, n - m)}$, where $\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i} = \{\mathbf{z} \in \{0, 1\}^{n-1} : \Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}) > 0\}$ is the support of $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$. [From the proof: Supplement A, p. 9] Let $t_i(\mathbf{z}) = \sum_{j \ne i} I_{ji}z_j$ be the element sum of $\mathbf{z} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{-i}$, and let $T_i = \sum_{j \ne i} I_{ji}Z_j$ be the element sum of $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ (i.e., the number of treated units interfering with $i$, excluding $i$ itself). [pp. 9-10] $\frac{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z} \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i} = \mathbf{z})} = \frac{\Pr(T_i = t_i(\mathbf{z}) \mid Z_i = z)}{\Pr(T_i = t_i(\mathbf{z}))}$.
canonical_claim.note: Sol's smallest repair: replace the draw size $\reflectbox{c}_i$ by $r_i = \reflectbox{c}_i - 1$ in both laws and in every ratio identity, and treat $r_i = 0$ separately. Everything is exact for fixed $n$. The passage from the scalar ratio to the vector ratio of the lemma is the identity quoted in the definitions (each pattern with $t$ ones on the $r_i$ units has unconditional probability $\binom{n - r_i}{m - t}\binom{n}{m}^{-1}$ and conditional probability $\binom{n - 1 - r_i}{m - z - t}\binom{n - 1}{m - z}^{-1}$). The validator checked the whole chain in rational arithmetic for all $2 \le n \le 40$. Lemma A14 and Proposition 3 use only the stated inequality.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Lemma A7, first relation: '$e_{ij} = \sum_{\ell=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})I_{\ell i}I_{\rho(\ell)j}$', as printed
canonical_claim.location: Supplement A, proof of Lemma A7: the sentence beginning 'Definition 7 gives', foot of p. 5 and top of p. 6. Definition 7: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed step] [Supplement A, pp. 5–6] PROOF. The proof follows a similar structure as the proof of Lemma 1. Definition 7 gives $e_{ij} = \sum_{\ell=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})I_{\ell i}I_{\rho(\ell)j} \le \sum_{\ell=1}^{n} I_{\ell i}I_{\rho(\ell)j}$. [What is refuted] The equality: by Definition 7, $e_{ij}$ is the indicator that some $\ell$ has $(1 - d_{ij})I_{\ell i}I_{\rho(\ell)j} = 1$, not the number of such $\ell$. [Counterexample, from the validator] $n = 6$ with pairs $(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)$, that is $\rho(1) = 2$, $\rho(2) = 1$, $\rho(3) = 4$, $\rho(4) = 3$, $\rho(5) = 6$, $\rho(6) = 5$; interference indicators $I_{ii} = 1$ for all $i$, $I_{31} = I_{51} = I_{42} = I_{62} = 1$ and all others 0. The units interfering with unit 1 are $\{1, 3, 5\}$ and those interfering with unit 2 are $\{2, 4, 6\}$, so $d_{12} = 0$. The terms $(1 - d_{12})I_{\ell 1}I_{\rho(\ell)2}$ equal 1 for $\ell = 1, 3, 5$ and 0 for $\ell = 2, 4, 6$. Hence $e_{12} = 1$ while $\sum_{\ell=1}^{6}(1 - d_{12})I_{\ell 1}I_{\rho(\ell)2} = 3$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplement B, Section 1.4: the closed form $B_2 = \frac{\lfloor a_n \rfloor(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}{n + \lfloor a_n \rfloor(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}$, as printed
canonical_claim.location: Supplement B, p. 8, Section 1.4: the display after 'It follows that' giving $B_2$, and the display after 'Taken together, we can conclude that'
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [Supplement B, p. 8] Taken together, we have $B_2 = \frac{1}{n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}}\sum_{i=2}^{\lfloor a_n \rfloor}\sum_{j=2}^{\lfloor a_n \rfloor}\mathbb{1}[i \ne j]\mathrm{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j \mid Z_i = 1, Z_j = 1)$. Conditional on $Z_i = 1$, we have $Y_i = 2Z_1 + X_i + \varepsilon_i$ for all $2 \le i \le a_n$. Hence, for all $2 \le i \ne j \le a_n$, $\mathrm{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j \mid Z_i = 1, Z_j = 1) = 4\mathrm{Var}(Z_1) = 1$. It follows that $B_2 = \frac{\lfloor a_n \rfloor(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}{n + \lfloor a_n \rfloor(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}$. To ease the exposition in this illustration, we will assume that the potential outcome for unit 1 is such that $X_1 + \varepsilon_1 = -1/4$, in which case $B_1 = \frac{(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}{n + \lfloor a_n \rfloor(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}$. [...] Taken together, we can conclude that $n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})\right] \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \frac{n - (\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1) - \lfloor a_n \rfloor(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}{n + \lfloor a_n \rfloor(\lfloor a_n \rfloor - 1)}$. canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] [Supplement B, p. 3] The bias is negligible relative to the variance for the settings and sample sizes we consider here. [What is refuted] The sentence for the settings with complete interference ($a_n = n$) under complete and paired randomization with the unweighted balance function, which the tables include. [Counterexample, from the validator] Let $n$ be even, $G_i = \mathbf{U} \setminus \{i\}$ for every $i$, and $b_i = X_i + \varepsilon_i$ any fixed numbers. Let the design be complete randomization with $n/2$ treated units, or paired randomization for any pairing $\rho$. Then, for every assignment $\mathbf{Z}$ in the support of the design: (a) $\sum_j Z_j = n/2$, so $\mathrm{bal}(G_i) = \sum_{j \ne i}(2Z_j - 1) = 1 - 2Z_i$, and $Y_i = b_i$ for every unit (the branch $\mathrm{bal}(G_i) < 0$ if $Z_i = 1$; the branch $\mathrm{bal}(G_i) > 0$ with $z_i = 0$ if $Z_i = 0$); (b) $\tau_i(\mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = 2(1 - Z_i)$, so $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z}) = \frac{2}{n}\sum_i(1 - Z_i) = 1$ and $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = 1$; (c) $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2Z_i - 1)b_i$; (d) $\Pr(Z_i = 1) = \frac{1}{2}$, so $\mathrm{E}[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}] = \mathrm{E}[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}] = 0$: the bias with respect to EATE is exactly $-1$ for both estimators, for every even $n$ and every $b_1, \ldots, b_n$. Hence the squared bias divided by the variance is $\frac{3n}{58}$ under complete randomization and tends to infinity under both designs, and the mean square error about EATE is the variance plus 1.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Remark 2: the value of $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}$ for a design that assigns the same treatment to all units, corrected
canonical_claim.location: p. 688 (PDF p. 16), Remark 2, fourth sentence. Definition 9: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)
canonical_claim.statement: [Printed statement] REMARK 2. If no units interfere, $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ is constant at zero, and Assumption 6 is trivially satisfied. However, no interference does not imply that Assumption 5 holds. Consider a design that assigns the same treatment to all units: $Z_1 = Z_2 = \cdots = Z_n$. The external mixing coefficient would not be zero in this case; in fact, $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} \to n/4$. [Corrected statement] For a common assignment with $\Pr(Z_1 = 1) = p$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = (n - 1)p(1 - p) = \Theta(n)$; in particular, for $p = 1/2$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} \sim n/4$. [In full] Suppose no units interfere, so $I_{ij} = d_{ij} = \mathbb{1}[i = j]$, and the design is $Z_1 = Z_2 = \cdots = Z_n = T$ with $T \sim$ Bernoulli($p$), $0 < p < 1$. Then for $i \ne j$, $\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j) = \alpha(T, T) = p(1 - p)$, and with mixing exponent $\theta = (q - 2)/q \in [0, 1]$ in Definition 9, $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j \ne i}[p(1 - p)]^{\theta} = (n - 1)[p(1 - p)]^{\theta}$. Under no interference and Assumption 1 the potential outcomes are uniformly bounded ($|y_i(z)| \le k^{3/2}$), so the maximum $q$ of Definition 9 is unbounded and $\theta = 1$: $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = (n - 1)p(1 - p)$. For $p = \frac{1}{2}$ this is $\frac{n - 1}{4}$, so $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}/(n/4) \to 1$; for $p = \frac{1}{3}$ it is $\frac{2(n - 1)}{9}$, which is not asymptotic to $n/4$. In every case $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}$ is of order $n$ and Assumption 5 fails, as the remark concludes.

canonical_claim.statement: [Printed step] [Supplement A, p. 37] The Bernoulli design and Assumption 1 imply that the support of $\mathbf{z}'$ consists of $2^{b_n}$ points each with a probability of at least $k^{-b_n}$. It follows that: $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left(f_n^*(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{SUB},n}) = 1\right) = \alpha/2$ and $\lim_{n \to \infty}\Pr\left(f_n^*(\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{SUB},n}) = -1\right) = \alpha/2$. [Corrected step] The Bernoulli design and Assumption 1 imply that the support of $\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{SUB},n}$ consists of $2^{b_n}$ points, each with probability at most $(1 - 1/k)^{b_n} \to 0$. Hence disjoint sets can approximate the two target masses $\alpha/2$, and the minimizing $f_n^*$ has both stated limits. [In full] (i) Under a Bernoulli design with $k^{-1} \le p_i \le 1 - k^{-1}$, every point $\mathbf{a} \in \{0, 1\}^{b}$ satisfies $k^{-b} \le \Pr((Z_1, \ldots, Z_b) = \mathbf{a}) \le (1 - 1/k)^{b}$. When we change $i$'s assignment, those units will change to $\mathrm{bal}(G_j) = 1$, and thus change the values of their outcomes. The consequence is that when we change $i$'s assignment from control to treatment and add one to $\mathrm{bal}(G_j)$ for the units in $\mathcal{G}_i$, a counteracting effect happens because we simultaneously change $\ell$'s assignment from treatment to control and remove one from $\mathrm{bal}(G_j)$ for units in $\mathcal{G}_\ell$. The number of units that get one added to $\mathrm{bal}(G_j)$ will, with high probability and relative to the sample size, be close to the number of units that get one removed.
